title: Tilenus holds this immortality natural rather than supernatural, yet by God's covenant, not the body's own power
source_text: XXIII. Caeterum istam immortalitatem quae homini in integritate primigenia competebat, pertendunt dici debere potius naturalem quam supernaturalem, & revera primum hominem aliquo sensu fuisse natura immortalem. Haec est doctrina Tileni Disputationis modo citatae Thesi octava. Ubi asserit hominem vere dici natura immortalem. Thesi tamen secunda mentem suam distinctius explicans, docet corpus primi hominis per se quidem fuisse corruptibile, quippe ex contrariis, & inter se pugnantibus qualitatibus conflatum: Veruntamen ex Dei pacto incorruptibile fuisse futurum, si homo in Dei obsequio constitisset sine peccato.
pass_a_gloss: But they contend that that immortality which belonged to man in his primeval integrity ought to be called natural rather than supernatural, and that in truth the first man was in some sense immortal by nature. This is the doctrine of Tilenus in the Disputation just cited, eighth Thesis. Where he asserts that man is truly called immortal by nature. Yet in the second Thesis explaining his mind more distinctly, he teaches that the body of the first man was indeed of itself corruptible, being compounded of contrary and mutually conflicting qualities: But that by God's covenant it would have been incorruptible, if man had stood in God's obedience without sin.
pass_b_english: The Reformed, however, maintain that the immortality man had in his first integrity should be called natural rather than supernatural, and that the first man really was in some sense immortal by nature. This is what Tilenus teaches in the eighth thesis of the disputation just cited, where he says that man is truly called immortal by nature.

Yet in the second thesis, explaining his meaning more precisely, he teaches that the first man's body was in itself corruptible, since it was made up of contrary qualities in conflict with one another, but that by God's covenant it would have been incorruptible had man continued in obedience to God without sin.

choices.why: The implied subject is the Reformed doctors of thesis XIX; the English names them so the turn from Rome is clear.
